articles.title: Timing of vaccine-associated anaphylaxis and implications for post-vaccination observation period: A systematic review and Canadian surveillance data analysis.
articles.summary: PMID: 42981916. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129303. BackgroundThe post-vaccination observation period ensures the rapid identification and clinical management of immediate adverse events following immunization, including anaphylaxis. Recommended observation periods vary internationally. In Canada, a 15 min observation period is standard. This systematic review assesses the empirical basis for these recommendations and the potential impact of varying observation period durations.ObjectiveTo describe time to onset of anaphylaxis following immunization and provide an empirical basis to evaluate variable post-vaccination observation period durations.MethodsThis study combined mixed methods to capture the available evidence base. A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines searched Embase and MEDLINE from inception to March 6, 2023, for studies reporting time to onset of anaphylaxis within 30 min of vaccination. Anaphylaxis reports submitted to the Canadian Adverse Events Following Immunization Surveillance System (CAEFISS) were also analyzed.ResultsOf 44 studies reporting 1365 cases of anaphylaxis, 1229 (90%) had recorded onset time, of which 802 (65%) occurred within 30 min. Among cases with sufficient temporal detail (n = 305), 236 (77%) had onset within 15 min; of 113 cases with 5-min interval data, 61% had onset within 5 min. Findings were broadly consistent across COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 vaccines, age groups, and levels of diagnostic certainty. Among 2193 CAEFISS reports, the median onset time was 12 min; 78% (n = 1702) occurred within 30 min, 80% (n = 1363) of which occurred within 15 min, and 46% (n = 628) of those within 5 min. Results were similar across age groups and vaccine types.ConclusionsVaccine-associated anaphylaxis most commonly presents within 15 min of vaccination. A routine 15-min observation period would be expected to capture most (77-80%) events occurring within 30 min.

articles.title: The Brighton collaboration standardized module for mpox vaccines, MVA-BN and LC16m8, benefit-risk assessment.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008353. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129253. Based on the rapidly evolving multi-country outbreak in Africa, WHO declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) from August 2024 to September 2025. In this outbreak, to date, over 100,000 suspected mpox cases and 1700 deaths have been reported from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The MVA-BN and LC16m8 mpox vaccines have been recommended by WHO, the MVA-BN vaccine was WHO prequalified and the first shipment of donated vaccine arrived in DRC in Sept 2024. DRC launched the first phase of the mpox vaccination campaign in October 2024 with the MVA-BN vaccine and both vaccines have been used to help control the outbreak. The benefit-risk assessment (BRA) for the MVA-BN and LC16m8 mpox vaccines on "Myocarditis following MVA-BN, and the LC16m8 Mpox vaccines: A Case Study based on global data" was prepared by the authors on an urgent basis for the DRC national regulatory authority, the Congolese Pharmaceutical Regulatory Authority (ACOREP), in September 2024. The module was developed to help guide the utilization of the donated mpox vaccines in DRC and was prepared utilizing publicly available data from epidemiological studies, clinical trials, post-marketing studies and real-world evidence. The analysis was conducted for all WHO recommended schedules for the vaccines, including the MVA-BN vaccine administered subcutaneously and intradermally (as a dose-sparing option), for pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, for adults and immunocompromised adults and LC16m8 vaccine administered to adults. The BRA was repeated in 2026 as there was additional data on the vaccines available. The base case of mpox incidence in the updated analysis was the annualized incidence of mpox reported in DRC from January 2024 through March 2025 (from the beginning to the main peak of the epidemic in DRC). High and low incidence were 10 x and 1/10 of the base rate, respectively, incidence rates that were considered so that the BRA is useful for different incidence rates during the outbreak, among different risk groups, and for different regions of the country. The results of the analysis were similar. The benefits of the MVA-BN vaccine administered subcutaneously or intradermally, for pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), for children and adults, including immunocompromised individuals and one dose of LC16m8 vaccine administered to >1 year of age strongly outweighed the risks for the base and base x 10 incidence rates and marginally for the base/10 incidence rate. The updated analysis is presented in this publication.

articles.title: Immunogenicity and safety of two priming doses of an MF59-adjuvanted cell-based H5N8 influenza vaccine in healthy persons aged ≥18 years.
articles.summary: PMID: 42998534. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129279. BackgroundIncreased transmission of avian influenza from animals to humans has elevated the risk of an H5 pandemic.MethodsThis phase 2, randomized, observer-blind, multi-center trial assessed the immunogenicity and safety of homologous priming with an MF59-adjuvanted, cell-based H5N8 A/Astrakhan/3212/2020 clade 2.3.4.4b vaccine (aH5N8c). We enrolled adults age ≥18 years, equally stratified into 18-64 (including a poultry-worker subset) and ≥65 year cohorts. Primary and secondary outcomes were homologous antibody responses against H5N8 measured in all participants by hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and in a subset by microneutralization (MN) assays on Days 1, 22, and 43. Solicited adverse events (AEs) were monitored for 7 days post-vaccination, with unsolicited AEs tracked throughout Day 43.Results239 participants were vaccinated (18-64 years, n = 121; ≥65 years, n = 118). At Day 43 (21 days post second aH5N8c dose), geometric mean fold increases (GMFI) were 13.7 for the 18-64 cohort and 10.2 for the ≥65 cohort. HI seroconversion rates were 75.8% (95% CI 66.1-83.8%) for the 18-64 cohort and 71.0% (61.1-79.6%) for the ≥65 cohort. HI titers ≥1:40 were achieved in 75.8% (66.1-83.8%) and 73.0% (63.2-81.4%) of participants, respectively. MN seroconversion rates were 80.6% (68.6-89.6%) and 70.0% (56.8-81.2%), while MN titers ≥1:40 were 83.9% (72.3-92.0%) and 86.7% (75.4-94.1%), respectively. No notable differences in immune responses by poultry worker status were observed. Most solicited AEs were mild or moderate, resolving within 3 days. Unsolicited AEs were reported by 16.7% participants by Day 43.ConclusionThese data support the use of the MF59-adjuvanted, cell-based monovalent H5N8 vaccine as a public health intervention against H5 influenza.

articles.title: Understanding COVID-19 vaccine concerns among adults with diabetes at federally qualified health centers: a qualitative analysis of open-ended survey responses.
articles.summary: PMID: 42994120. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129333. AimsAdults with diabetes mellitus (DM) have higher risks for COVID-19-related morbidity and mortality. This qualitative study analyzed why some adults with DM at federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) declined to receive a COVID-19 vaccine during the COVID-19 pandemic.MethodsA COVID-19 outcomes/vaccination uptake survey was administered to adults with type 1 and type 2 DM on insulin therapy at 33 FQHCs from Nov. 2021-Jul. 2022 as part of a larger study. We cross-sectionally and thematically analyzed open-ended responses from participants that explained why they did not receive a COVID-19 vaccine. Responses were coded using the 3 Cs of Vaccine Hesitancy Model (complacency, confidence, and convenience reasons). Responses that did not match the 3 Cs were coded as "other" or "unspecific" reasons for vaccine hesitancy/refusal. Descriptive statistics (n, %, mean, standard deviation [SD]) summarized participant demographics and codes.ResultsOut of 450 survey participants, 80 (17.8%) reported not receiving a COVID-19 vaccine; of those, 67 participants (mean age = 46.6 years [SD ± 15.1], 65.7% female, 49.3% White) reported 80 total reasons for being unvaccinated. Most reflected low confidence (38.8%), such as distrust in vaccines, distrust in the health system and government, and concerns tied to misinformation, or were unspecific (35.0%). Convenience reasons (13.8%) included vaccine inaccessibility, vaccine ineligibility e.g., due to medical contraindications, and dislike of vaccines. Complacency reasons (8.8%) included low perceived susceptibility/threat from COVID-19 and perceived vaccine ineffectiveness. Other reasons (3.8%) included religious beliefs and personal freedom.ConclusionsThis study demonstrates that multi-level factors contributed to COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy/refusal among adults with DM at FQHCs. Tailored vaccine education, improved vaccine communications, and multifaceted interventions are needed to address their vaccine concerns.

articles.title: Changes in childhood vaccination coverage and sociodemographic determinants across Nigerian states, 2018-2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 42998535. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129317. BackgroundNigeria accounts for a substantial share of the world's zero-dose children and exhibits marked subnational disparities in childhood vaccination coverage. Although national estimates indicate modest gains in full vaccination, less is known about how vaccination outcomes and their determinants have changed across states over time, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines factors associated with changes in full vaccination coverage and zero-dose prevalence across Nigerian states between 2018 and 2024.MethodsWe conducted a repeated cross-sectional, state-level ecological analysis using data from the Nigeria Demographic and Health Surveys conducted in 2018 and 2024. Outcomes were full vaccination coverage and zero-dose prevalence among children aged 12-23 months. State-level sociodemographic, governance, and health system indicators were drawn from survey, administrative, and budget data. Ordinary least squares regression models assessed cross-sectional associations and relationships between changes in vaccination outcomes and explanatory variables over time.ResultsMean full vaccination coverage increased from 33.0% in 2018 to 40.8% in 2024, while zero-dose prevalence rose from 14.1% to 24.2%. Geographic disparities persisted, with states experiencing high zero-dose prevalence in 2024 often showing the largest increases since 2018. Maternal education was consistently associated with higher full vaccination coverage and lower zero-dose prevalence. In 2024, higher state health budgets, greater trust in local government, and COVID-19-related service disruptions were associated with higher full vaccination coverage.ConclusionsDespite modest national gains, zero-dose prevalence increased and disparities widened. Institutional factors appear increasingly important, underscoring the need for targeted, state-specific strategies to reach zero-dose children.

articles.title: Effectiveness of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine against Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations among U.S. veterans: An observational study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43002871. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129254. BackgroundSARS-CoV-2 continues to cause clinically important morbidity, but Covid-19 vaccine effectiveness can vary across seasons as circulating variants, vaccine antigen composition, population immunity, and immunization policy change. During 2025-2026, peak Covid-19 hospitalization rates were lower than in the preceding season, making the absolute benefit of vaccination especially important for clinical and policy decisions. We estimated the effectiveness of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine against Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations among US veterans.MethodsWe emulated a target trial using electronic health records from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Adults aged 18 years or older who received a 2025-2026 seasonal influenza vaccine between Sept 21, 2025, and Jan 31, 2026, were eligible. Same-day coadministration of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 and influenza vaccines was compared with influenza vaccination alone; recipients of influenza vaccine alone were censored if they subsequently received a 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine. Outcomes were Covid-19-associated emergency department visit, Covid-19-associated hospitalization, and their composite. Per-protocol vaccine effectiveness and risk differences per 10,000 persons at 180 days were estimated with inverse-probability-of-treatment-weighted and inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted discrete-time survival models.FindingsAmong 931,943 participants, 114,911 received same-day Covid-19 and influenza vaccines and 817,032 received influenza vaccine alone. Over 180 days, Covid-19 vaccination was associated with lower risks of Covid-19-associated emergency department visits (vaccine effectiveness 31.72%, 95% CI 17.58 to 43.03; risk difference - 7.04 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -10.34 to -3.63), Covid-19-associated hospitalizations (vaccine effectiveness 43.57%, 95% CI 16.12 to 62.10; risk difference - 2.63 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -4.52 to -0.83), and the composite outcome (vaccine effectiveness 32.72%, 95% CI 18.94 to 43.82; risk difference - 7.41 per 10,000 persons, 95% CI -10.75 to -3.99).InterpretationIn this national cohort of US veterans presenting for seasonal influenza vaccination, receipt of the 2025-2026 Covid-19 vaccine was associated with lower risks of Covid-19-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations. Absolute risk reductions were modest, but they quantify the benefit of vaccination in a lower-incidence season and can inform shared clinical decision making and seasonal vaccine policy.FundingUS Department of Veterans Affairs.

articles.title: Investigating predictors of pertussis vaccination in pregnancy across England: cross sectional studies of maternity staff and mothers.
articles.summary: PMID: 42987448. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129309. IntroductionPertussis vaccination is recommended for all pregnant women in England. Uptake remains suboptimal, with regional and demographic variability, leaving neonates at risk. This persists despite expansion of vaccine provision across maternity services since 2017. This study aimed to identify determinants of inequity and opportunities for intervention.MethodsCross-sectional online surveys of: ii) 551 maternity healthcare professionals (HCPs), comparing those working in trusts within the highest- and lowest-vaccinating regions of England. i) 377 mothers of young babies from lowest-vaccinating regions, comparing women vaccinated versus unvaccinated against pertussis in their recent pregnancy; and Questionnaires were informed by the COM-B framework. Logistic regression modelling assessed factors associated with vaccination, alongside content analysis of free-text responses.Resultsi) HCP survey: Area-level deprivation was strongly associated with low-vaccinating regions. Controlling for this, low-vaccinating regions were associated with HCPs' lower confidence in vaccine discussions and more perceiving these as burdensome, greater desire for training, and increased perceived responsibility for vaccination. Free-text responses described midwifery culture of providing vaccination information neutrally, avoiding direct recommendations in favour of supporting women's choice. ii) Mothers' survey: Most mothers (90%) rated HCPs as influential in their vaccination decision. Non-vaccination (20% of sample) was most strongly associated with lack of awareness that pertussis vaccination was recommended and lack of conviction that their midwife supported vaccination. Main reasons for vaccination were safety for the baby and HCP recommendation. Clear midwife recommendation was associated with satisfactory perceptions of vaccine communication across groups. The importance of access was commonly recognised but did not differentiate between groups in either study.ConclusionsMidwives need support to avoid a neutral stance and provide clear, confident recommendations, including infant safety reassurance. Funding models should account for deprivation, not solely service size, to help reduce vaccination inequity.

articles.title: Strengthening catch-up vaccination delivery in routine health services for children under five in Western Kenya, 2022-2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008350. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129330. BackgroundCatch-up vaccination can close population immunity gaps, yet integration into routine immunization services remains limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Following Kenya's 2023 catch-up vaccination policy, we evaluated a multi-strategy intervention to strengthen systematic identification, eligibility screening, and delivery of missed doses within routine health services in Siaya County.MethodsOver 12 months, five strategies addressing healthcare worker (HCW) capacity, vaccination documentation, defaulter tracking, immunization screening, and caregiver engagement were implemented in 55 public health facilities selected through stratified random sampling. Using a pre-post design, we assessed immunization uptake, missed opportunities for vaccination (MOVs), and system readiness. Baseline (November 2022-January 2023) and endline (October-December 2024) evaluations included facility assessments, HCW interviews, caregiver exit surveys among children aged <36 months with home-based records (HBRs; n = 658), and facility immunization register abstractions (n = 1650 children aged 12-23 months). Analyses accounted for sampling design, clustering, and used generalized estimating equations for HBR data.ResultsMOV prevalence among children visiting facilities for any reason declined from 94.4% to 20.9% (p < 0.001). Full immunization among children aged 12-23 months increased from 44.9% to 63.6% (p < 0.001), with uptake improving across antigens. Measles-rubella first-dose uptake increased from 51.5% to 78.0%, and second-dose uptake from 18.8% to 36.9% (p < 0.001 for both). Eligibility screening expanded from 60.6% to 86.8% of facilities (p = 0.012), defaulter tracking improved from 48.5% to 91.6% (p < 0.001), and HCW knowledge and confidence increased significantly.ConclusionThe multi-strategy intervention was associated with fewer MOVs and improved uptake, suggesting that embedding catch-up vaccination within routine health services can strengthen immunization systems in decentralized LMIC contexts. Kenya's catch-up vaccination policy provided a framework for introducing catch-up vaccination into routine health services.

articles.title: Hepatitis A vaccination coverage among adolescents aged 13-17 years, United States, 2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43019905. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129343. BackgroundHepatitis A is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that causes inflammation of the liver. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) incrementally expanded childhood hepatitis A (HepA) vaccine recommendations from 1996 to 2006, the year when universal childhood vaccination was recommended. In 2020, ACIP recommended catch-up vaccination for children and adolescents aged 2-18 years who had not previously received HepA vaccine at any age.MethodsWe analyzed data from the National Immunization Survey-Teen (NIS-Teen) to assess HepA series initiation (1-dose) and completion (≥ 2-doses) among adolescents aged 13-17 years in the United States during 2024, identify factors associated with HepA series completion among adolescents, and evaluate changes in HepA vaccination coverage among adolescents since the 2020 ACIP catch-up vaccination recommendation by comparing NIS-Teen data from 2019 to data from 2024.ResultsIn 2024, national HepA vaccination coverage among adolescents was 91.8% (95% CI, 91.1%, 92.5%) for series initiation and 87.1% (95% CI, 86.1%, 88.0%) for series completion. Jurisdiction-level ≥ 2-dose coverage ranged from a low of 71.2% in Mississippi (95% CI, 63.9%, 77.6%) to a high of 97.5% in Georgia (95% CI, 93.4%, 99.1%). Adolescents who received an 11-12-year-old well child exam or checkup, saw a physician at least once during the past 12 months, had a mother aged ≥45 years, or had a mother with at least some college education were significantly more likely to have received ≥2 doses of HepA vaccine. Compared to 2019, significant increases occurred among U.S. adolescents in both HepA series initiation (7.4 percentage point [pct pt] increase in 1-dose coverage) and series completion (9.9 pct pt increase in ≥2-dose coverage) in 2024 (p < .05).ConclusionHepA vaccination coverage improved among U.S. adolescents following the introduction of the 2020 ACIP catch-up vaccination recommendation.

articles.title: Childhood pneumococcal conjugate vaccination in Aotearoa New Zealand and the delayed indirect effects on older populations: a population-based surveillance cohort study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008352. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129342. BackgroundIn Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ) there have been multiple changes to the childhood pneumococcal vaccine schedule since 2008 when PCV7 was first introduced. Most recently PCV13 was reintroduced in late 2022 after 5 years of PCV10. In the present study, we investigate the shifts in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) incidence rates attributed to PCV-specific serotypes.MethodsWe report PCV-specific trends in IPD, PCV-specific vaccine impact (VI) by age group, and report the timing for expected reductions in PCV13-specific (non-PCV7 serotypes) IPD for children under 5 and adults 65 or over.FindingsIPD incidence rates in NZ are at historically high levels for adults 65 or over, while rates for children under 2 and 2-4 years old have dropped significantly since the re-introduction of PCV13. Māori and Pacific peoples are experiencing the highest rates of IPD since 2009. The percent of IPD cases attributed to PCV13-specific serotypes has decreased across all age groups, while the percent of cases attributed to PCV20-specific serotypes has increased for most age groups. The VI of PCV13 was 79% (95% CI 59-90%) for children under 2 years of age. Similarly, the timing of a 50% decrease in risk for PCV13-specific (non-PCV7 serotypes) IPD was very rapid for children under 2 (within 1 year) and delayed for adults.InterpretationThough overall incidence rates of IPD remains very high, this is driven primarily by non-PCV serotypes. The VI for all PCVs remains high, especially for younger cohorts. Delayed indirect benefits are continuing to be experienced by older populations.FundingThe NZ Ministry of Health funds IPD surveillance in NZ.

articles.title: Defining and validating an HPV vaccination motivation score in Kenya and Malawi: A tool for use in low- and middle-income countries.
articles.summary: PMID: 42994119. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129325. BackgroundStudies have evaluated reasons for low HPV vaccine uptake globally but use instruments that were validated only in high-income countries. Our objectives were to (1) determine factors associated with vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) in two low- and middle-income countries; and (2) use them to develop and validate a simple score to measure motivation to vaccinate one's daughter against HPV.MethodsWe undertook 3 rounds of data collection: Kenya 2022 (1345 parents/guardians of girls aged 10-16 years, via nationwide mobile phone random-digit dialing), Malawi 2022 (288 parents/guardians of girls aged 9-13 years, via household surveys in three communities), and Kenya 2024 (re-survey of 678 Kenya 2022 respondents who reported having no vaccinated daughters in 2022). The survey included items from the Vaccine Hesitancy Scale-Child and Vaccine Hesitancy Scale-HPV, the Human Papillomavirus Attitudes and Beliefs Scale, and the Wellcome Global Monitor, and parent-reported HPV vaccination of eligible girl(s) in the household.ResultsWe found four latent constructs significantly associated with vaccination status in the Kenya 2022 data: Confidence in Vaccine Benefits, Safety Concerns About the HPV Vaccine, Talks About HPV With Others, and Perceives Pro-HPV Vaccination Social Norms. We use these to create an HPV Vaccination Motivation Score; in the Malawi 2022 data (external validity), a 3-point increase in this score was associated with greater odds of having a vaccinated daughter (OR = 1.55; p < 0.0001), and in the Kenya 2024 data (predictive/temporal validity), a 3-point increase in the score was associated with significantly greater odds of vaccination in the intervening two years (OR = 1.14; p = 0.0008).ConclusionsThis HPV Vaccination Motivation Score can be used to investigate factors associated with HPV vaccination in diverse global settings - and this information can be used to design more effective interventions and programs to increase vaccine coverage and improve health outcomes.

articles.title: A modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) virus vectored Zika vaccine that generates neutralising antibodies and potent T cell responses in type I interferon deficient mice.
articles.summary: PMID: 42994118. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129269. To date, no vaccine has been approved against Zika virus (ZIKV). Any such vaccine must be safe to use during pregnancy and needs to consider immune interactions from prior flavivirus exposure given these viruses co-circulate and share the same mosquito vector. To address these issues, we have developed a vaccine using a modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) virus. Here, we describe the development of this MVA vectored Zika vaccine that encodes structural proteins, premembrane and envelope, and non-structural (NS) proteins, NS3 and NS5 (MVA-ZIKA-B). A two-dose vaccination regimen with MVA-ZIKA-B resulted in significant serum neutralising activity and induced polyfunctional T cell responses that protected in a mouse model of Zika, rendering virus undetectable across multiple tissues after virus challenge. Vaccine-associated protection was also characterised by high IgG antibodies against the ZIKV envelope and potent interferon-gamma (IFNγ)-positive T cell responses when stimulated ex vivo with ZIKV peptides. Further stability studies showed that the vaccine antigens were stably expressed, and the vaccine progressed to GMP manufacturing. A phase I human trial with MVA-ZIKA-B is ongoing.

articles.title: mRNA-LNP vaccines targeting mutation-derived BRCA2 and p53 elicit antigen-specific immune responses in beagles.
articles.summary: PMID: 43019901. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129347. Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines are next-generation platforms capable of eliciting potent cellular and humoral immunity through intracellular expression of tumor-associated or mutation-specific antigens. The resulting mRNA-LNP formulations, namely canine BRCA2-10204ins candidates (cBR2-Cand), canine BRCA2-p53 28-mer epitopes (cBR2-p53), and canine BRCA2-partial (cBR2-Part), were then admixed to prepare the cBR2-cocktail, a mixed mRNA-LNP vaccine designed to enhance mutation-specific immune responses. In vitro expression was confirmed in HeLa cells. In vivo immunization in mice induced strong interferon (IFN)-γ secretion, particularly against BRCA2 H143R, K801R, and T1425P mutations. Beagles immunized with cBR2-cocktail mRNA-LNPs exhibited increased IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells after repeated dosing, without significant hematological or biochemical abnormalities. Mutation-derived mRNA-LNP vaccines safely induced mutation-specific T-cell responses in vivo. Although anticancer efficacy was not assessed, we established a preclinical foundation for developing mutation-targeted mRNA immunotherapies for CMT and underscored the translational relevance of the canine model for human BRCA2/p53-related cancers.

articles.title: HPV vaccination initiation among preadolescents in Veneto, Italy: associations with chronic conditions and socioeconomic disadvantage.
articles.summary: PMID: 43019904. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129345. BackgroundIdentifying population groups with lower human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination uptake is essential for developing targeted public health interventions. This study examined whether chronic conditions and sociodemographic factors were associated with HPV vaccination initiation among preadolescents in the Veneto Region of Italy.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from Pedianet, an Italian primary-care pediatric database. The study included children born between 2008 and 2011 who were followed between 9 and 12 years of age. Vaccination initiation was defined as receipt of at least one HPV vaccine dose from the ninth birthday to the day before the thirteenth birthday. Associations with sex, birth cohort, selected chronic conditions, disability, income-based healthcare exemption, and pediatric healthcare utilization were assessed using multivariable multilevel logistic regression, with a random intercept for family pediatrician.ResultsAmong 19,245 children followed by 93 pediatricians, 53.6% received at least one HPV vaccine dose. Asthma was associated with higher odds of vaccination initiation (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.36; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12-1.67), whereas disability (aOR 0.71; 95% CI 0.58-0.88), income-based healthcare exemption (aOR 0.81; 95% CI 0.76-0.86), and male sex (aOR 0.79; 95% CI 0.74-0.84) were associated with lower odds of initiation. Associations with receipt of two HPV vaccine doses within the same age window were broadly consistent with those for initiation.ConclusionsHPV vaccination initiation was associated with health-related and sociodemographic factors. Lower uptake among children with administratively recognized disability, those with income-based healthcare exemptions, and boys identifies groups that may benefit from targeted vaccination support. Further research should clarify the barriers underlying these associations.

articles.title: Discrepancy between cross-neutralizing reactivity and protection in horses suggests inactivated vaccine antisera underestimate cross-protection against equine influenza.
articles.summary: PMID: 43019903. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129339. For equine influenza vaccine strain selection, antisera collected from infected horses (post-infection antisera) have been used for antigenic analysis. However, inactivated whole-virus vaccines are widely administered to horses, and therefore, the use of antisera collected from horses immunized with inactivated viruses (inactivated vaccine antisera) has the potential to be more clinically relevant for evaluating vaccine efficacy. The objective of this study was to determine whether inactivated vaccine antisera can serve as a reliable surrogate for post-infection antisera and whether they are appropriate for equine influenza vaccine strain selection. In the virus neutralization assay, post-infection antisera against a Japanese vaccine strain (A/equine/Ibaraki/1/2007) cross-reacted with the heterologous challenge strain (A/equine/New York/1/2017), whereas inactivated vaccine antisera showed a more than 10-fold reduction in cross-reactivity. However, in the experimental challenge study with A/equine/New York/1/2017, horses immunized with inactivated A/equine/Ibaraki/1/2007 showed significantly reduced rectal temperature, virus shedding, and inflammation marker levels, despite low cross-neutralizing reactivity, when compared to the unimmunized control horses. These results indicate that a reduction in cross-neutralizing reactivity of inactivated vaccine antisera does not necessarily reflect a loss of vaccine efficacy in horses. In conclusion, this study suggests that relying only on inactivated vaccine antisera underestimates vaccine efficacy against equine influenza. Although preparing post-infection antisera presents practical difficulties, their use remains valuable for the selection of appropriate vaccine strains.

articles.title: Factors associated with TAK-003 dengue vaccine acceptance among Thai adults using the Health Belief Model and Theory of Planned Behavior in a tertiary care hospital.
articles.summary: PMID: 43014059. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129332. Although the live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine (TAK-003) is now available in Thailand, evidence on the behavioral determinants of its acceptance remains limited. We assessed TAK-003 vaccine acceptance, identified factors associated with acceptance using the Health Belief Model and Theory of Planned Behavior frameworks, and evaluated willingness to pay. We conducted a cross-sectional survey from December 2025 to February 2026. Thai adults aged 18-60 years who had never received a dengue vaccine were included and recruited through convenience sampling at Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok. Factors associated with vaccine acceptance were identified using multivariable binary logistic regression. A total of 448 participants were included, of whom 46.7% (n = 209) accepted the TAK-003 vaccine. In the adjusted model, participants aged 50-60 years (adjusted Odd ratio (aOR) = 2.61, 95% CI: 1.33-5.11), those with a history of dengue infection (aOR = 2.61, 95% CI: 1.56-4.35), greater perceived susceptibility (aOR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.02-2.41), greater perceived benefits (aOR = 2.57, 95% CI: 1.44-4.60), stronger cues to action (aOR = 2.33, 95% CI: 1.20-4.55), and more positive attitudes toward the vaccine (aOR = 1.74, 95% CI: 1.06-2.84) were significantly associated with vaccine acceptance. articles.title: HLA-A*11:01-restricted CD8<sup>+</sup> T-cell responses induced by conserved epitope vaccination confer cross protection against heterologous challenge in mice.
articles.summary: PMID: 43014058. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129318. The rapid antigenic drift of influenza surface glycoproteins frequently causes "antigenic mismatch," severely compromising seasonal vaccine efficacy. To address this, we evaluated an immunization strategy wherein quadrivalent inactivated vaccine (QIV) pre-immunization is followed by a multi-epitope peptide boost. This peptide mixture comprises highly conserved, HLA-A*11:01-restricted CD8+ T-cell epitopes from internal viral proteins (NP, M1, PB1). In HLA-A*11:01 transgenic (Tg) mice, this QIV/5Pep-Mix regimen selectively amplified measurable, epitope-specific IFN-γ+ CD8+ T-cell responses. Following lethal heterologous challenge with the PR8 strain, the peptide-immunized Tg mice achieved 100% survival, accelerated weight recovery, reduced pulmonary viral titers, and attenuated lung histopathology. Crucially, this cross-protection was primarily driven by CD8+ T-cell-mediated immunity, as humoral cross-reactivity (HAI, IgG, neutralizing antibodies) against PR8 was negligible. Furthermore, protective efficacy was completely abolished in wild-type mice, confirming strict dependence on HLA-A*11:01 presentation. These findings demonstrate that an epitope-based "add-on" strategy effectively bridges the gap left by strain-mismatched antibody responses. This approach offers a promising platform for universal influenza vaccines in high-frequency HLA populations, providing a reliable second line of defense against seasonal drift and pandemics.

articles.title: Recombinant Newcastle disease virus expressing Anatid herpesvirus-1 glycoprotein C as a vaccine candidate for ducks.
articles.summary: PMID: 43008351. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129338. Duck plague, caused by Anatid herpesvirus-1 (AnHV-1), remains a significant threat to waterfowl production, while recombinant vaccine strategies against the disease remain limited. Here, we constructed a recombinant Newcastle disease virus expressing the AnHV-1 glycoprotein C (rNDV-gCA) using reverse genetics and assessed its biological properties and immunogenicity. The recombinant virus was rescued and showed stable expression of gC while retaining replication kinetics similar to rNDV. Cytokine profiling revealed robust induction of type I cytokines and decreased expression of pro-inflammatory mediators compared with the control, indicative of a balanced innate immune response. Consistent with these findings, stimulation of duck peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with rNDV-gCA enhanced the expression of antiviral mediators. Furthermore, conditioned supernatants from stimulated chicken PBMCs induced an antiviral state in recipient chicken embryonic fibroblast cells and reduced AnHV-1 replication. The effect is more pronounced following exposure to rNDV-gCA-derived supernatants compared to wtAnHV-1 and rNDV. The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, western blot, hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, and virus neutralization test (VNT) were used to investigate humoral immunity in rNDV-gCA-vaccinated ducks. The recombinant virus eliciting gC- and AnHV-1-specific antibodies with measurable virus-neutralizing activity. Together, these results establish that rNDV-gCA is a stable and immunogenic recombinant virus in vivo and provide proof of concept for the use of rNDV as a vector for in vivo delivery of AnHV-1 antigens.
